claims.text: Near-equiatomic multi-element nanoparticles have high configurational entropy.
High configurational entropy creates a sluggish-diffusion effect in multi-element nanoparticles.
Sluggish diffusion impedes atomic rearrangements and phase segregation.
Impeded atomic rearrangement and phase segregation preserve nanoparticle structural integrity and chemical composition under service conditions.
Uniformly mixed, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles with multiple metal elements can be prepared.
Making the nanoparticles off-equiatomic reduces their configurational entropy.
Local atomic arrangements elevate barriers to atomic diffusion.
Elevated diffusion barriers delay grain growth.
Elevated diffusion barriers delay phase separation.
Elevated diffusion barriers delay changes in surface composition.
High configurational entropy raises the activation energy for atomic migration.
Higher atomic-migration barriers suppress phase segregation and sintering at elevated temperature.
Near-equiatomic nanoparticles will exhibit less grain growth than off-equiatomic nanoparticles after identical thermal exposure.
Near-equiatomic nanoparticles will exhibit less phase segregation than off-equiatomic nanoparticles after identical thermal exposure.
Near-equiatomic nanoparticles will exhibit smaller surface-composition changes than off-equiatomic nanoparticles after identical thermal exposure.
Reduced structural and chemical changes will preserve catalytic activity and thermoelectric properties closer to their initial values.
Off-equiatomic nanoparticles will have faster atomic diffusion and more pronounced structural and chemical degradation under the same thermal conditions.
The proposed entropy-mediated mechanism will dominate at 773–1173 K for catalytic use and 473–1923 K for thermoelectric use in inert or controlled atmospheres.
Reactive gas environments, support interactions, partial oxidation, or extreme pressures may alter the proposed stability mechanism.
